newsitem.title: USA: Cominco fined for pollution at Red Dog Mine.
newsitem.headline: Cominco fined for pollution at Red Dog Mine.

text.p: Cominco Alaska Inc. agreed Monday to pay $1.7 million in civil penalties and to spend $3 million in environmental improvements to settle pollution charges arising from its Red Dog Mine in northwestern Alaska.
The mine, the world's largest lead and zinc producer, violated water-pollution laws for a four-year period ending in 1993, said the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The settlement and the complaint that listed the Clean Water Act charges were filed Monday in U.S. District Court in Anchorage, EPA said, adding that the negotiations took three years.

"The agreement with Cominco puts the violations behind us and marks the start of some ambitious efforts by the company to help make sure no harm comes to the aquatic resources on which native Alaskans depend," Chuck Clarke, EPA's Pacific Northwest regional director, said in a news release.

Those projects include long-term groundwater and permafrost monitoring to determine whether any pollution seeped from the mine's tailings pond, a barrier to protect fish populations from mine discharges, and a study to determine whether discharges have harmed marine life.
EPA said developing and installing the groundwater and permafrost monitoring equipment will be the most expensive improvement, with a cost of $2.7 million, according to Cominco's estimates.

Before the settlement was reached, Cominco made significant improvements at the mine and brought it into compliance with wastewater-discharge permit requirements, said Joe Roberto, an EPA compliance officer.
The company installed a sand-filter system, a project initially estimated to cost $3.2 million, and improved its system for treating sanitary wastes, at an estimated cost of $340,000, Roberto said.
Cominco was not immediately available for comment.
The Cominco-operated Red Dog Mine is located above the Arctic Circle on land owned by an Inupiat Eskimo group.
The Inupiat group, NANA Regional Corp., is one of 12 for-profit regional corporations set up by the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act.
